config.title: Kindergeld in Berlin - FAQ
config.subtitle: How much Kindergeld is, how far back it is paid, which residence permits carry the entitlement, and where the Berlin Familienkasse sits.

items.q: How much is Kindergeld in Berlin in 2026?
items.a: **259 euros a month for every child**, since January 2026. It was 255 euros in 2025 and 250 euros from 2023. The amount is the same for a first child and a fifth, and it does not depend on what the parents earn. Berlin has no separate rate: this is federal money paid by the Familienkasse Berlin-Brandenburg.

items.q: How far back will the Familienkasse pay if I apply late?
items.a: **Six months, and not one month more.** Section 70 (1) of the Income Tax Act limits the payout to the six months before the beginning of the month in which your application arrives. Apply in September and you are paid from March. On 1 October, March drops out and April becomes the oldest month you can reach. Six months at the current rate is **1,554 euros**.

items.q: It used to be four years. When did that change?
items.a: On **1 January 2018**. The Steuerumgehungsbekämpfungsgesetz of 23 June 2017 replaced the old four-year reach with the six-month window for every application filed from that date. The rule was later moved into section 70 of the Income Tax Act, where it sits now.

items.q: Can I claim Kindergeld on a student or job-seeking residence permit?
items.a: Not on the permit alone. Section 62 (2) names permits under sections 16b, 16d, 16e, 19c, 19e, 20 and 20a (5) of the Residence Act as exceptions. You do qualify if you are **actually employed or self-employed**, on **Elternzeit**, or drawing benefits under **Book III of the Social Code**. A settlement permit, an EU long-term residence permit or a work-bearing permit such as the Blue Card carries the entitlement by itself.

items.q: My children live in another EU country and I work in Berlin. Can I still claim?
items.a: Yes. Working in Germany is enough to open the entitlement even when the children live in another EU or EEA state. The family benefit paid in their country is set against the German amount and you receive the difference, which is usually called Differenzkindergeld.

items.q: What do I actually need to apply?
items.a: Your own **Steuer-Identifikationsnummer** and the **child’s**, the birth certificate, and for a non-EU applicant the residence permit. For a child over 18, add the school certificate, enrolment paper or Ausbildung contract. A missing tax ID is the single most common reason an application stalls, and the Bundeszentralamt für Steuern will resend it on request.

items.q: Where is the Familienkasse in Berlin?
items.a: The Familienkasse Berlin-Brandenburg posts from Potsdam and keeps three counters in the city: **Charlottenstr. 87 to 90**, **Storkower Str. 120** and **Sonnenallee 282**. They open **Tuesday 09:00 to 12:00** and **Thursday 09:00 to 12:00 and 14:00 to 18:00**. The free line is **0800 4 5555 30**, and the online service handles most cases without a visit, including a fully paperless application for a newborn.

items.q: Do I have to reapply when the amount goes up?
items.a: No. The Familienkasse raises the amount by itself and pays the new rate from January. Nothing has to be sent in. You only need to tell them when something changes: a move, a new bank account, a child leaving education, or a separation.

items.q: What else can I claim alongside Kindergeld?
items.a: **Kinderzuschlag** adds up to **297 euros a month per child** for parents who earn enough for themselves but not for the children, with an income floor of 900 euros gross for a couple and 600 euros for a single parent. The **Kinderfreibetrag** is 9,756 euros in 2026 and the Finanzamt automatically applies whichever of the two leaves you better off. On top of that, Berlin gives a free Kita place from the age of one, a free school ticket, and from 1 August 2026 an eight-hour all-day place for first-year primary pupils.
